slides.say: A baker has chocolate and vanilla cupcakes. She sells one third of the chocolate cupcakes and one sixth of the vanilla cupcakes, always selling whole cupcakes. The cupcakes left are ten of one flavor and fourteen of the other, in an unknown order. How many cupcakes did she have at first?

The hard part here is that we don't know which leftover belongs to which flavor. So we'll simply check both options. We'll solve it two ways, the math way checking both options, and then with an estimate.

Let's start with the math way. She sold a sixth of the vanilla cupcakes, so what's left of the vanilla is five sixths. Let's say fourteen vanilla cupcakes are left. Then fourteen is five sixths of the vanilla.
at: so what's left of the vanilla

slides.say: Five sixths are fourteen cupcakes, so one sixth would be fourteen divided by five. That's not a whole number. But she sells only whole cupcakes, so one sixth must be a whole number of cupcakes. So fourteen can't be the vanilla.

slides: So it's the other way round. Ten vanilla cupcakes are left, and fourteen chocolate.

slides.say: First the vanilla. Ten cupcakes are five sixths of the original vanilla total. So one sixth is ten divided by five, two cupcakes. She sold one sixth, so we give it back. Six sixths are six times two, twelve vanilla cupcakes.
at: Six sixths are six times two

slides.say: Now the chocolate. She sold a third, so two thirds are left. Fourteen cupcakes are two thirds of the original chocolate total. So one third is fourteen divided by two, seven cupcakes. Three thirds are three times seven, twenty-one chocolate cupcakes.
at: So one third is fourteen divided by two

slides.say: At first she had twelve plus twenty-one, thirty-three cupcakes. Choice number four is our answer.
at: Choice number four is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Now let's estimate, and we don't even care which pile is which. We start again from the givens. Ten plus fourteen is twenty-four cupcakes left.
She sold a third of one flavor and a sixth of the other. That's not much, so she started with a bit more than twenty-four. Let's check the choices.

Choice number two, twenty-six. She sold at least a sixth of every flavor, so at least a sixth of all the cupcakes. A sixth of twenty-six is more than four. So more than four were sold, and fewer than twenty-two would be left. But twenty-four are left. Out.
at: at least a sixth of all

slides.say: Choice number one, forty-eight. She sold at most a third of every flavor, so at most a third of all. A third of forty-eight is sixteen. So at least thirty-two would be left, not twenty-four. Out.
And choice number three, seventy-two, is even bigger, so even more would be left. Out too. Only thirty-three is left. Choice number four is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
at: so even more would be left
Choice number four is our answer
